children: By Amanda Lee and Edith Hancock
The European Union and the Philippines struck a "substantial" agreement on a free-trade deal, as persistent geopolitical shocks and tariffs underscore the need to look for new trade partners.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she reached the agreement with Philippines President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Tuesday, a milestone that followed her visit to the Southeast Asian country three years earlier to relaunch negotiations.
The two sides aim to deepen bilateral trade and investment and the deal is now on a path toward formal conclusion in the coming months.

EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters on Tuesday that both sides agreed to liberalize more than 94% of tariff lines covering more than 97% of trade. "This is very good news, and a major opening for EU exporters who already sell over 8 billion euros [$9.17 billion] a year" to the Philippines in goods from machinery and medicines to pork and dairy, he said.

The Brussels-Manila deal aims to deliver new opportunities for businesses--especially small and medium firms--more jobs, and stronger supply chains at a time when resilience has become a strategic priority. The EU commission said in a statement that the agreement would also touch on government procurement contracts, intellectual property, digital trade and sustainability agreements.

In 2025, the EU was the Philippines' fourth-largest trading partner, accounting for 8.3% of the country's total trade in goods. The Southeast Asian nation's top exports to the trading bloc include electronic products and agricultural goods.
The EU's commission has ramped up efforts to bolster ties with other countries in a bid to curb reliance on the U.S. and China.

Earlier this year, the EU inked a landmark agreement with India and has progressing trade agreement negotiations in various phases with Malaysia and Thailand. An India-New Zealand FTA is due to come into force next month.

Canada, which is in the midst of a tit-for-tat tariff tiff with Washington, is turning to Asia too. Earlier this week, a top Canadian trade official met with his India counterpart in Mumbai to discuss strengthening trade and investment ties.

In a post on X, Canadian Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu said that after "a successful round of negotiations with India," he was now traveling to the Philippines for the Asean Economic Ministers' Meeting to advance talks on free trade agreements with both the Philippines and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which includes 11 member states.
In 2025, Canada's bilateral merchandise trade with Asean rose 24% to 52.4 billion Canadian dollars, equivalent to US$37.33 billion.

Trade uncertainty has been a persistent theme in foreign relations this year since a U.S. Supreme Court ruling struck down many of the tariffs the Trump administration had levied on economies last year over trade imbalances. Since then, the U.S. government has continued pursuing tariffs via other routes.
